name: South Sudanese Asida
description: Asida, a stiff sorghum porridge, is genuinely South Sudan's primary staple - even ahead of kisra, which is the second staple - real technique beating real sorghum flour into boiling water until it forms a smooth, cohesive dough eaten by hand alongside stews.
steps_detailed: Whisk about a third of the sorghum flour with the salt into 1.25 cups boiling water.
Gradually beat in the remaining flour, stirring vigorously, over medium-low heat 15-18 minutes, until very thick and smooth.

name: South Sudanese Kombo (Okra and Sesame Stew)
description: Kombo, also called swala, is a real okra soup thickened distinctively with real ground sesame paste, giving South Sudanese soups their genuinely distinctive silky texture, different from peanut-based versions found elsewhere in the region.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Seeds, sesame seeds, whole, roasted and toasted

ingredients.ingredient: Seeds, sesame seeds, whole, roasted and toasted

steps_detailed: Brown the chicken, 6-7 minutes.
Add the tomatoes and simmer 8-10 minutes.
Whisk the ground sesame with a little water into a smooth paste and add to the pot along with the okra.
Simmer 15-18 minutes until the chicken is tender and the stew turns silky from the sesame and okra together.

name: South Sudanese Kuindiong
description: Kuindiong is a cherished Dinka welcome dish with a real two-part technique that was missing here before: butter and yogurt are cooked together separately until they visibly separate and the yogurt solids turn a pale, nutty brown (called miok), while the semolina cooks into a pudding in its own pot with yogurt and water - the finished pudding is then topped with spoonfuls of the separately-made miok, not mixed together as one step.
steps_detailed: For the miok topping: melt half the butter in a small pan, stir in half the yogurt, and cook, stirring constantly, 15-18 minutes, until the mixture boils and the yogurt solids separate from the fat and turn a pale, nutty brown. Set aside.
For the pudding: bring 1 cup water to a boil, then slowly stir in the remaining yogurt.
Reduce heat and gradually whisk in the semolina, stirring constantly until it thickens into a smooth pudding.
Stir in the milk, sugar, and remaining butter, and cook 1-2 minutes more.
Serve the pudding topped with spoonfuls of the separately-made miok.

name: South Sudanese Royoroyo
description: Royoroyo, a real specialty of Yei town traditionally cooked for honored guests, is genuinely built on roasted pigeon peas as its base, not ground peanuts and sesame alone as this was described before - real technique stirs the peanut butter and sesame butter in gently at the end, deliberately not fully combining them, so the natural oils visibly separate from the pea base rather than blending into a smooth sauce.

ingredients_full.ingredient: Seeds, sesame seeds, whole, roasted and toasted

ingredients.ingredient: Seeds, sesame seeds, whole, roasted and toasted

steps_detailed: Cook the pigeon peas in water until tender, 25-30 minutes, then drain, reserving a little of the cooking liquid.

Return the peas to low heat and gently stir in the peanut butter and ground sesame paste, stirring only enough to combine loosely - real technique deliberately avoids fully blending them, so the natural oils separate from the peas rather than forming a smooth sauce.
Season with salt and cook 8-10 minutes more, stirring gently, adding a splash of the reserved liquid if needed.

name: South Sudanese Kisra
description: Kisra, a thin, fermented sorghum flatbread, is South Sudan's second staple after asida, shared with neighboring Sudan, real technique spreading the fermented batter thin like a crepe.
steps_detailed: Whisk the sorghum and all-purpose flour with water and the vinegar into a thin, pourable batter.
Let ferment at room temperature 8-12 hours to develop real tang.
Pour a thin layer onto a hot, lightly greased griddle, spreading thin like a crepe, and cook 1-2 minutes per side.

name: South Sudanese Ful Medames
description: Ful medames, slow-cooked fava beans, is a beloved breakfast staple shared across the wider Sudanese and Sahel region.
steps_detailed: Simmer the fava beans with a splash of water, 8-10 minutes, until very soft.
Mash roughly and stir in the garlic, lemon juice, and olive oil.

Add the okra and simmer 6-8 minutes until tender.

name: South Sudanese Grilled Fish
description: Grilled fish, fresh from the White Nile, is a genuine South Sudanese staple, real technique keeping the seasoning simple to let the fresh fish carry the dish.
steps_detailed: Rub the fish with the garlic and lemon juice, and let sit 10 minutes.
Grill or broil, 4-5 minutes per side, until just cooked through.

name: South Sudanese Molokhia
description: Molokhia, a garlicky, silky green soup, shared with Egypt and Sudan, real molokhia leaf isn't a distinct item here, so spinach stands in.
steps_detailed: Simmer the chicken in the broth 20-22 minutes until tender, then shred and reserve the broth.
Blend the spinach until finely chopped.
Cook the garlic in a little oil 1 minute, then add the spinach and reserved broth.
Simmer 10-12 minutes, then return the shredded chicken.
